# Section 1

## Part 1: Authentication

### Explanation

I registered at [nhgis.org](https://uma.pop.umn.edu/nhgis/user/new) and generated an API key at [account.ipums.org](https://account.ipums.org). I then set it in my R environ and assigned it a key name for later use.

```{r}
#| message: false

#load the package into the session
library(ipumsr)

#set API key 
usethis::use_git_ignore(".Renviron")
usethis::edit_r_environ()

#retrieve the key in R 
ipums_key <- Sys.getenv("IPUMS_API_KEY")

#check whether R found it, run:

ipums_key != ""


```

## Part 2: The Data Challenge

### Explanation

I used the [NHGIS Data Finder](https://data2.nhgis.org/) to locate and verify that the desired table **NP1** in the **1990_STF1 data set**. I first downloaded an initial zip using the websites filtering options to look at what kind of data I should expect. I then used the provided **IPUMS** functions to download and read the file directly into R as a data frame.

```{r}

#| label: extract-data

#define function
extract_state_pop_status <- define_extract_agg(
  collection = "nhgis",
  description = "1990 State Total Population (NP1)",
  datasets = ds_spec(
    name = "1990_STF1",
    data_tables = "NP1",
    geog_levels = "state"
  )
)

#submit
submit_extract <- submit_extract(extract_state_pop_status)


#wait & download extract
wait_extract <- wait_for_extract(submit_extract)
download_file <- download_extract(wait_extract)

#read Zip into a data frame
raw_state_pop <- read_nhgis(download_file)

raw_state_pop

```

## Part 3: Data Cleaning

### Explanation

I used **dplyr** functions **select** and **rename** to clean the data. I noticed that several columns only had NAs and columns 33 through 37 were not used. So i used that information to write my select arguments.

```{r}
# use var info to check var names
ipums_var_info(raw_state_pop)

#select and rename
tidy_state_pop <- raw_state_pop |> 
                    select(where(~ !anyNA(.x)), -(33:37)) |> 
                    rename(gisjoin = GISJOIN,
                           year = YEAR,
                           state_abbr = STUSAB,
                           division = DIVISIONA,
                           region = REGIONA,
                           state_name = STATE,
                           state_code = STATEA,
                           land_area = AREALAND,
                           water_area = AREAWAT,
                           total_pop = ET1001)
tidy_state_pop
```

## Part 4: Find the population density

### Explanation

I used **dplyr** function **mutate** and **the provided formula** to calculate population density, but I needed to convert the land_area column into numeric first.

```{r}

#use mutate to calculate population density, land_area convereted to numeric 
state_density <- tidy_state_pop |>
                  mutate(land_area = as.numeric(land_area), 
                    pop_density = total_pop /land_area)
                  
state_density |> select(year, 
                        state_name, 
                        land_area, 
                        total_pop, 
                        pop_density) |> 
                  head(10)
```

## Part 5: Find Water Share

### Explanation

I used **dplyr** function **mutate** and **the provided formula** to calculate water_share, but I needed to convert the water_area column into numeric first.

```{r}
#use mutate to calculate water share, water_area convereted to numeric 
water_share <- state_density |> 
                mutate(
                  water_area = as.numeric(water_area), 
                  water_share = (water_area)/(land_area + water_area)
                )
water_share |> select(year, 
                        state_name, 
                        land_area, 
                        water_area, 
                        water_share) |> 
                head(10)
```

# Section 2

## Part 1 : Scrape data

### Explanation

I used **rvest** to scrape the data and **janitor** to do initial cleaning of names. However more cleaning was needed in step 2 because the first raw was still data and not header. I was also surprised my preferred piping method `|>` did not work for selecting the first table but `%>%` did. If though reverting to `%>%` worked this time, I will read more about when to use each one to make sure

```{r}

#load library
library(rvest)
library(janitor)

#define url
url <- "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population"


pop_rank_raw <- read_html(url) |> 
  html_table(header = TRUE) %>%            # scrapes all tables      
  .[[1]] %>%                              # selects the first table
  as_tibble(.name_repair = "unique") |>   # fixes empty column names
  clean_names()                           # cleans to snake_case 

pop_rank_raw
```

## Part 2: Clean and standardize the data

### Explanation

I used **slice** to remove the first raw and referenced the column names generated by **colnames()** to rename the variables into descriptive names.

```{r}

#look up colnames for reference
colnames(pop_rank_raw)

# remove first raw and rename columns
pop_rank_2 <- pop_rank_raw |> 
  slice(-1) |> 
  rename (
    rank = x1, 
    state = state_or_territory,
    total_pop_2025 = census_population_8_9_a_3,
    total_pop_2020 = census_population_8_9_a_4,
    house_seats = house_seats_b_5, 
    pct_seats = house_seats_b_6, 
    pop_per_seat_2020 = pop_perseat_2020_a, 
    pop_per_ev_2020 = pop_perelec_vote_2020_c, 
    pct_us_pop_2020 =  percent_us_2020, 
    pct_ec_2020 = percent_ec_2020
    
  )
pop_rank_2
```

## Part 3: Correct column classes

### Explanation

I used **mutate** to to change the class of rank to integer and all the other variables except for **state** name to numeric. State was already character class and it needed to stay that way. **parse_number** does a nice job of **removing commas** and **percentage signs** as it converts the characters to numerical values.

```{r}

# covert rank to integer and all but the state names as numeric.
pop_rank_3 <- pop_rank_2 |> 
              mutate(
               rank = as.integer(rank),
               across(3:10, ~ parse_number(.x))
  )
pop_rank_3
```

## Part 4: Handle missing values

### Explanation

When i looked at the tibble, there were no similar placeholders, but just to be safe i run the following script to convert any place holders with with `NA`.

```{r}
pop_rank_4 <- pop_rank_3 |> 
  # Replace common placeholder strings with true R NAs across your character columns
  mutate(across(where(is.character), ~ na_if(.x, "-"))) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.character), ~ na_if(.x, "N/A"))) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.character), ~ na_if(.x, "")))
pop_rank_4
```

## Part 5: Final verification

### Explanation

I checked for duplicated rows and the number of rows matches the number of U.S. states + territories. I removed the last 4 rows because they were not particular state or territory data but aggregate.

```{r}

#find any completely identical duplicate rows
duplicated_rows <- pop_rank_4 |> 
  get_dupes()

# check total number of rows
total_rows <- nrow( pop_rank_4)
print(total_rows)

#remove last 4 rows that are not US state or territory
pop_rank_tidy <- pop_rank_4 |> 
  slice(-(57:60))

pop_rank_tidy
```
